lesson.title: The Turning Point Nobody Expected
lesson.summary: In late January 1968, North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launched a massive, coordinated surprise assault across South Vietnam during the Tet lunar new year holiday, and although it ended in a military defeat for the attackers, it shattered American confidence that the war was close to being won.
lesson.body:
By early 1968, US military and political leaders had spent months assuring the American public that the war in Vietnam was being won and that North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces were nearing exhaustion. That confidence was upended in the early hours of January 30 and 31, 1968, when North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launched coordinated attacks on more than a hundred cities, towns, and military installations across South Vietnam, timed to the Tet holiday, the Vietnamese lunar new year, during what had traditionally been an informal truce.

The attacks reached places Americans had been told were secure. Viet Cong fighters breached the outer wall of the US Embassy compound in Saigon, and communist forces seized and held the old imperial city of Hue for nearly a month before being driven out in brutal, block by block fighting. Militarily, the offensive was a disaster for the attackers. American and South Vietnamese forces beat back the assaults everywhere and inflicted casualties heavy enough to cripple the Viet Cong as an effective fighting force for years afterward.

Yet the political effect ran in exactly the opposite direction. The scale, coordination, and sheer audacity of the Tet Offensive directly contradicted the optimistic picture the Johnson administration and General Westmoreland had been presenting, and television coverage brought scenes of fighting in the streets of Saigon into American living rooms. A credibility gap that had already been widening between the government's public statements and the war's realities on the ground now became impossible for many Americans, including previously supportive members of the press and political establishment, to ignore.

The political fallout was swift. Johnson's approval ratings collapsed, and on March 31, 1968, he announced in a televised address that he would limit further bombing of North Vietnam, pursue negotiations, and not seek reelection that year. Tet did not end the war, which would grind on for years, but it marked the moment when a majority of the American public and much of Washington stopped believing that victory was near, giving new energy and legitimacy to a growing anti-war movement.
